name: Heap Validity Check (is this array a valid max/min heap)
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek array diya hai aur poocha hai ye valid max-heap/min-heap represent karta hai ya nahi — seedha parent-child comparison check karna hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Check parent(i) vs children(2i, 2i+1) at EVERY internal node — max-heap needs parent≥both children, min-heap needs parent≤both.
Remember: NO left-vs-right ordering requirement, only parent-vs-children.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. For each index i from 1 to ⌊n/2⌋ (all internal nodes), check array[i] against array[2i] and array[2i+1] (if they exist).
2. A single violation anywhere disqualifies the array as a valid heap of that type.
commonTraps: Checking only the root, or only a few positions, instead of ALL internal nodes.

name: Build-Heap / Heapify (converting an arbitrary array into a heap)
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek arbitrary (non-heap) array diya hai aur poocha hai minimum interchanges/swaps kitne chahiye ise max/min-heap banane ke liye, ya build-heap ki complexity kya hai — ye is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (30 me se 5 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: Build-heap goes BOTTOM-UP: start sift-down from the LAST internal node (index ⌊n/2⌋), work backward to the root.
Total build-heap time is O(n), NOT O(n log n) — a classic surprising result.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify the last internal node (index ⌊n/2⌋ in 1-indexed array).
2. Sift-down at that node (swap with larger/smaller child if violated, repeat down the path) — count actual swaps.
3. Move to the PREVIOUS internal node, repeat, all the way up to the root.
4. Sum all actual swaps performed for the 'minimum interchanges' answer.
variationsObserved: Only the ROOT violates heap property (rest of tree already valid) — special case, single sift-down from root suffices, O(log n) not O(n).
commonTraps: Trying top-down insert-one-at-a-time instead of bottom-up sift-down — gives a different (and for this specific counting question, WRONG) interchange count.
Assuming build-heap is O(n log n) instead of the correct O(n).
edgeCases: When only the root is unbalanced (rest already a valid heap), the fix is a single O(log n) sift-down, not a full O(n) rebuild.

name: Insertion into Heap (bubble-up trace)
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek existing heap (array/level-order form) di hai, aur ek (ya do) naye elements INSERT karne hain — poocha hai resulting heap kya hoga.
whatShouldComeToMind: Place new element at the next leaf position (end of array, maintaining completeness), then bubble UP: swap with parent while parent is violated.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Append the new element at the next available array position.
2. Compare with its parent; if heap property violated, swap.
3. Repeat comparing-and-swapping with the new parent until property holds or root is reached.
4. If inserting multiple elements, repeat the whole process for each one IN ORDER.
commonTraps: Forgetting to re-check the heap property after EACH individual insertion when multiple elements are inserted in sequence.

name: Deletion from Heap (sift-down trace)
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek existing heap se DELETE operation(s) perform ki gayi hain (usually extract-root, ya delete an arbitrary indexed node) — poocha hai resulting array kya hoga.
whatShouldComeToMind: Standard delete-root: move the LAST array element to the root position, shrink array size by 1, then sift-down from root.
Delete an ARBITRARY node (not root): replace it with the LAST element, then it might need to sift EITHER up or down (check both directions) to restore the property.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Replace the deleted node's slot with the array's last element, shrink the array.
2. Compare the moved element with its children — sift DOWN if it's now too small (max-heap) for its position.
3. If deleting a non-root node, ALSO check against its new parent — sift UP if it's now too large for its new position.
variationsObserved: Two consecutive delete operations — trace them sequentially, don't try to shortcut.
commonTraps: Forgetting to check BOTH sift-up and sift-down directions when deleting a non-root node (arbitrary-position deletion).

name: Finding the Opposite Extreme (min-in-max-heap or max-in-min-heap)
recognitionClueHinglish: Max-heap me MINIMUM (ya min-heap me MAXIMUM) dhundhna hai — poocha hai complexity kya hai. Ye is topic ka doosra bada pattern hai (30 me se 5 PYQs), ek specific counter-intuitive result.
whatShouldComeToMind: The opposite extreme MUST be at a LEAF (since every internal node is ≥/≤ its children, so it can't be the minimum/maximum respectively unless it's a leaf).
Must check ALL ⌈n/2⌉ leaves — Θ(n), can't do better.
conceptsRequired: Heap property implies opposite-extreme is always a leaf
Leaf-count in a complete binary tree
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify the leaf nodes (roughly the last half of the array, indices > ⌊n/2⌋).
2. Scan all of them, no shortcut — Θ(n) is both necessary and sufficient.
3. For 'number of possible index positions where the extreme COULD be' style questions, count the leaf range precisely.
variationsObserved: 'Number of possible positions for the maximum in a min-heap' — combinatorial counting of the leaf-index range, not a search algorithm question.
commonTraps: Assuming O(1) or O(log n) is achievable for this — it's fundamentally Θ(n) because the heap property gives NO information to narrow the search among leaves.

name: Array-Index Parent/Child Formulas (including d-ary heap generalization)
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai heap ke array-index se parent/child kaise nikaalein, ya d-ary heap (2 se zyada children per node) ka index formula/height/complexity poocha hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: d-ary heap: height reduces to O(log_d n), but each sift step now compares against d children instead of 2 — trade-off between tree height and per-node work.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Confirm indexing convention (0 or 1 based) from the question.
2. Apply the standard (or d-ary generalized) parent/child formula directly.
3. For complexity questions involving d, remember: insert/delete become O(d·log_d n) (d comparisons per level, log_d n levels).
commonTraps: Using the plain binary-heap formula for a d-ary heap question without adjusting for d.

name: Heap Structural Properties / Counting / Conceptual Claims
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai heap ki depth/height, ya 'how many distinct heaps possible' with a given value set, ya conceptual TRUE/FALSE statements (jaise 'second largest is always a child of root') — ye broader structural-property pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Second-largest in max-heap is ALWAYS one of root's 2 direct children — a direct heap-property consequence worth memorizing.

'Number of distinct heaps with n given distinct values' — count via the same recursive idea as counting binary tree shapes, but now ALSO accounting for which values can go where given the heap constraint (harder than BST counting since heap doesn't force a unique value-to-shape assignment).
generalSolvingApproach: 1. For TRUE/FALSE conceptual claims, trace back to the core heap property (parent≥/≤children) and verify directly, or find a small counterexample.

2. For counting-distinct-heaps questions, think recursively: choose which elements go in left vs right subtree (must respect relative size constraints), multiply by ways to arrange each subtree recursively.
variationsObserved: Height/depth of a specific-sized complete heap — direct ⌊log2 n⌋ computation.
Constructing a heap FROM a BST — reasoning about what's preserved/broken during the conversion.
commonTraps: Assuming the SECOND-largest could be anywhere — it's specifically constrained to be one of root's two children.
